questions.problem: A student who answers randomly has a $50%$ chance of correctly answering each question on a $12$-question test. What is the probability that the student selects exactly $10$ correct answers? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of correct answers that the student gets.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ questions

- the probability of hitting each question is $p=50%=0.5$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,0.5).$ We want to find the probability of getting $x=10$ correct answers.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=10) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{10})(0.5)^{10}(1-0.5)^{12-10} \\  & =\frac{12!}{10!(12-10)!}(0.5)^{10}(0.5)^{2} \\  & =66(0.5)^{10}(0.5)^{2} \\  & =0.016\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Ann has a collection of $20$ pairs of shoes, $12$ of which are sports shoes. Every working day she randomly picks a pair of shoes to go to work, and she has to work for $26$ days next month. What is the probability that she will choose a pair of sports shoes exactly $10$ times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of times Ann will choose a pair of sports shoes in those $26$ days.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=26$ working days next month

- since there are $12$ pairs of sports shoes out of $20$ pairs in the collection, the probability that she will pick a pair of sports shoes on a given day is

$$
p=\frac{12}{20}=\frac{3}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(26,\frac{3}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=10$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=10) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{26}{10}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{10}{(1-\frac{3}{5})}^{26-10} \\  & =\frac{26!}{10!(26-10)!}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{10}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{16} \\  & =\frac{26!}{10!16!}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{10}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{16} \\  & ≈0.014\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem: A box of chocolates contains cherry creams and almond little cakes in the ratio of $2:1.$ Four chocolates are selected at random, with replacement. What is the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of selected cherry creams.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=4$ selected chocolates

- since cherry creams and almond little cakes are in the ratio of $2:1,$ the probability of selecting a cherry cream from the box is $p=\frac{2}{3}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(4,\frac{2}{3}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(1-\frac{2}{3})}^{4-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting at most $2$ cherry creams. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4-2} \\  & =1{(\frac{2}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{4}+4{(\frac{2}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}+6{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\  & ≈0.407\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
An unfair coin has an $80%$ chance of landing on heads. The coin is tossed $5$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that the coin landed on heads at least four times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin landed on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ tosses.

- The probability of landing on heads is $p=80%=0.8.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.8).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.8)^{x}(1-0.8)^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.8)^{x}(0.2)^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that the coin landed on heads at least $4$ of the $5$ games. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 4) & =P(X=4)+P(X=5) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})(0.8)^{4}(1-0.8)^{5-4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})(0.8)^{5}(1-0.8)^{5-5} \\  & =5(0.8)^{4}(0.2)+1(0.8)^{5} \\  & ≈0.737,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places

questions.problem:
A wildlife camera detects animals with a $40%$ success rate. The camera is triggered $7$ times during the night. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that it detects an animal at least $3$ times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the camera successfully detected an animal.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=7$ triggers.

- The probability of detection is $p=40%=0.4.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(7,0.4).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.4)^{x}(1-0.4)^{7-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{7-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of detecting an animal at least $3$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 3).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 3)=P(X=3)+P(X=4)+…+P(X=7)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3) & =1-P(X<3) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{7-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{7-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{7-2}] \\  & =1-[(0.6)^{7}+7(0.4)(0.6)^{6}+21(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.419\,904 \\  & ≈0.580,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
